\[

\tag{9}

\[
\frac{1}{\#V_{p}(\mathbf F_{p})}
\sum_{x\in V_{p}(\mathbf F_{p})}

   = n \;+\; O\!\bigl(p^{-1/2}\bigr).
\tag{10}
\]

\[

\tag{11}
\]

\tag{12}

### 7.  Interpretation via Chebotarev and Burnside

A more elementary description uses Chebotarev’s density theorem.
Let \(\eta\) be the generic point of \(V\) and let

For each closed point \(x\in V\) with residue field \(\mathbf F_{p}\),

fundamental group maps to a conjugacy class in the geometric monodromy
group \(G=S_{n}\).  The number of \(\mathbf F_{p}\)-conics tangent to
the five conics parametrised by \(x\) is exactly \(\#\operatorname{Fix}
(\mathrm{Frob}_{x}\mid X)\).

Chebotarev says that, when we let \(p\) vary, the classes
\(\mathrm{Frob}_{x}\) become equidistributed in \(G\).  Therefore

\[
L = \frac{1}{|G|}
     \sum_{g\in G}\#\operatorname{Fix}(g\mid X).
\tag{16}
\]

Because the action is transitive, Burnside’s lemma gives

\[
\frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g\in G}\#\operatorname{Fix}(g) = 
\#\bigl(X/G\bigr)=1 .
\tag{17}
\]

Thus (16) again yields \(L=1\).  The same argument works for any
finite étale cover with transitive monodromy; the number 1 is the
*average number of rational points of a fibre*.

### 8.  Why the complement of \(V\) does not affect the limit

The definition of \(L\) in the problem uses only the open subset
\(V\subset U^{5}\) where \(\pi\) is finite étale.  The complement

\[

whereas \(\#V(\mathbf F_{p})\asymp p^{30}\).  Consequently the contribution
of points lying outside \(V\) to the average in (6) is at most
\(O(p^{-1})\) and disappears in the limit \(p\to\infty\).

\(\#V(\mathbf F_{p})\) grows like \(p^{25}\).

(If one prefers a more elementary viewpoint, one may replace the
geometric argument by the Chebotarev density theorem for the
étale fundamental group \(\pi_{1}^{\mathrm{ét}}(V)\).  The generic fibre
of \(\pi\) corresponds to a finite étale \(\pi_{1}^{\mathrm{ét}}(V)\)–
set of cardinality \(3264\); the average number of fixed points of the
Frobenius conjugacy class acting on this set is exactly the size of the
set, i.e. \(3264\).)

### 4.  Computing \(\bigl\lfloor 100L\bigr\rfloor\)

From (8),

\[
100L = 100\cdot 3264 = 326\,400 .
\]

Since the right–hand side is an integer,

\[
\Bigl\lfloor 100L \Bigr\rfloor = 326\,400 .
\]

\boxed{326400}

#### Remarks and further references

* The number \(3264\) appears in the classical problem *“five conics in the
plane”* (Chasles, 1865).  Modern treatments are given in
  *E. Kleiman – S. Laksov, “The enumerative theory of singularities”,
  Invent. Math. 1974*,
  *J. Harris, “Algebraic Geometry – A First Course”, Example 15.3*.

* The étale‑local description of \(\pi\) is a special case of a **Brill–
  Noether–type degeneracy locus** for a map of vector bundles on
  \(U^{6}\); its class is \(c_{5}\bigl(\mathcal E\bigr)\) where
  \(\mathcal E\) is a rank‑5 bundle whose fibres are the spaces of
  quadrics tangent to a given conic.  The top Chern class computes the
  degree \(3264\).

* The passage from the geometric degree to the average number of
  \(\mathbf F_{p}\)-rational conics is a standard “large‑\(q\)” principle,
  see N. Katz, *“Sums of Betti numbers in families”* (1999) or
  N. Katz–P. Sarnak, *Random matrices, monodromy and L‑functions*,
  Prop. 3.5.3.

* The hypothesis that the characteristic be different from \(2\) is essential:
  in characteristic \(2\) every smooth conic is a line pair after a
  purely inseparable base change, and the tangency divisor \(\mathcal D\)
  becomes non‑reduced.  The limit in the statement of the problem is
  taken over all primes, so the contribution of the finitely many bad
  primes is negligible.

Thus the enumerative geometry over \(\mathbf C\) controls the average
behaviour over finite fields, giving the simple numerical answer
\(326400\).
